title: Continuous Subarray Sum
description: Brute force to optimized: summing every subarray directly versus tracking prefix sums modulo k and detecting a repeated remainder at least 2 indices apart.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return true if nums has a contiguous subarray of size at least 2 whose elements sum to a multiple of k (0 is considered a multiple of every k), and false otherwise.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","nums, k"],["Output","true if a qualifying subarray exists, false otherwise"],["Goal","Decide this without checking every subarray's sum directly"],["Constraints","1 <= nums.length <= 100000; 0 <= nums[i] <= 100000000; 0 <= k <= 2^31 - 1"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["A subarray sum being \"a multiple of k\" is really a statement about remainders","Track prefix sums modulo k instead of the raw prefix sums"],["Two prefix sums with the SAME remainder mean everything between them sums to a multiple of k","A hashmap remembering the first index each remainder was seen at"]]}

blocks.text: Determine whether some contiguous stretch of at least 2 elements in nums adds up to an exact multiple of k.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding Two Odometer Readings That Land on the Same Lap Marker
blocks.text: Picture a circular track of length k, and a running total distance traveled marked at every step, wrapped around the track. If the running total lands on the exact same point on the track at two different steps, the distance traveled between those two steps is a whole number of complete laps, an exact multiple of k.

blocks.caption: A subarray sums to a multiple of k exactly when two prefix sums share the same remainder

blocks.text: The subarray [23,2,4] sums to 29... actually [2,4] sums to 6, an exact multiple of 6, so the answer is true.
The subarray [23,2,6,4,7] sums to 42, and 42 is a multiple of 6, so the answer is true.
Since only 0 itself is a multiple of 0, a qualifying subarray must sum to exactly 0, meaning it must consist of consecutive zeros of length at least 2.
Before summing every subarray directly, notice that "sums to a multiple of k" is a statement purely about remainders when divided by k, not about the actual sum value.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A subarray from index i plus 1 to j sums to prefix[j] minus prefix[i]; this difference is a multiple of k exactly when prefix[j] and prefix[i] have the SAME remainder modulo k.

Observation 2: So instead of tracking prefix sums directly, tracking prefix sums MODULO k is enough, and a repeated remainder at two positions signals a qualifying subarray between them.

Observation 3: Remembering only the FIRST index each remainder was seen at (not every occurrence) maximizes the distance between any repeat, which is exactly what is needed since the subarray must have length at least 2.

Observation 4: Seeding the hashmap with remainder 0 mapped to index -1 (representing an empty prefix before the array starts) correctly handles subarrays starting from index 0.
This leads to walking the array once, tracking the running sum modulo k, and checking a hashmap for whether that remainder has been seen at least 2 indices earlier.
Check every subarray of length at least 2 directly, summing it and testing divisibility by k.

items: For every starting index i, and every ending index j at least one position after i, sum nums[i..j] directly.
If that sum is a multiple of k (careful with k equal to 0), return true immediately.
If no subarray qualifies, return false.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: sum every subarray of length at least 2 directly, check divisibility

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every subarray of length at least 2 is checked directly, with its sum built incrementally as j grows.
k equal to 0 is special-cased, since checking divisibility by 0 is undefined; only an exact sum of 0 counts.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), every pair of start and end indices is examined.
Space: O(1).

Limitation: most subarray sums share the same remainder modulo k as some earlier prefix sum, but the brute force never tracks or reuses that information, re-summing from scratch for every starting index.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why re-summing every subarray is wasteful: a subarray sums to a multiple of k exactly when its two boundary prefix sums share the same remainder modulo k, a fact that can be checked with a single hashmap lookup instead of a fresh sum.

What to track while sweeping: the running prefix sum modulo k, and a hashmap remembering the FIRST index each remainder was seen at.

Why only the first occurrence matters: keeping the earliest index for each remainder maximizes the distance to any later repeat, giving the best chance of satisfying the "length at least 2" requirement, and is sufficient since any later repeat is at least as far as the first one.

The core idea: sweep once, tracking the running remainder, and return true the moment a remainder repeats at least 2 indices later than its first occurrence.

Seed a hashmap with remainder 0 at index -1. Sweep through nums, maintaining a running sum modulo k. If the current remainder has been seen before, check whether the current index is at least 2 more than the remembered index; if so, return true. Otherwise, if this remainder is new, record its index (only the first time it is seen).

blocks.content: {"headers":["Index","Running sum","Remainder mod 6","Seen before?"],"rows":[["-1 (seed)","0","0","recorded at index -1"],["0 (23)","23","5","new, recorded at index 0"],["1 (2)","25","1","new, recorded at index 1"],["2 (4)","29","5","seen at index 0; 2 - 0 = 2 >= 2, return true"]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: track the running remainder, check the hashmap for a distant repeat

blocks.text: If two prefix sums share the same remainder modulo k, their difference, the subarray between them, is exactly divisible by k. Recording only the FIRST index each remainder appears at ensures that any later repeat is checked against the earliest possible partner, maximizing the chance of the required length-2 gap, and any valid pair will be caught this way since if a later occurrence also repeats, the first occurrence is at least as far away.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), one pass with O(1) average hashmap operations.
Space: O(min(n, k)), since at most k distinct remainders can exist.

blocks.text: The key insight is reducing "sums to a multiple of k" down to "two prefix sums share the same remainder modulo k," turning a subarray-sum search into a simple repeated-remainder detection problem solvable with a single hashmap sweep.

items: Forgetting the length-at-least-2 requirement, and returning true for any repeated remainder regardless of distance.
Not seeding the hashmap with remainder 0 at index -1, which would miss valid subarrays starting at index 0.
Mishandling k equal to 0, where checking a remainder via modulo is undefined; only an exact sum of 0 should count.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["k = 0","Only two or more consecutive zeros qualify."],["A subarray sum of exactly 0 with k nonzero","0 is always a multiple of any nonzero k, so it always qualifies."]]}

blocks.text: Explaining the reduction, "same remainder at two prefix positions means the subarray between them is a multiple of k", up front is the clearest way to justify the hashmap-based approach before writing any code.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "can you avoid summing every subarray", think: track the running sum modulo k, and look for a repeated remainder far enough apart.

items: How would you find the actual subarray (not just whether one exists) once a qualifying pair of remainders is found?
How does this technique generalize to finding the LONGEST subarray summing to a multiple of k?
Subarray Sum Equals K, the same prefix-sum-plus-hashmap technique, applied to an exact target instead of a modular one.
Any "two prefix values sharing a property" counting or existence problem.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(n squared) time; the optimized running-remainder approach runs in O(n) time. Space is O(1) for the brute force and O(min(n, k)) for the optimized approach.

items: Pattern: prefix sums tracked modulo k, detecting a repeated remainder at least 2 indices apart.
Core Idea: a subarray sums to a multiple of k exactly when two prefix sums share the same remainder modulo k; track the first index of each remainder and check the gap on any repeat.
Time: O(n squared) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(1) for the brute force, O(min(n, k)) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: "sums to a multiple of k" reduces entirely to matching remainders between two prefix sums.
Interview Difficulty: the reduction itself is the key insight; correctly handling the length-2 requirement and k = 0 are the tricky details.
One line memory trick: same remainder at two prefixes, far enough apart, means a multiple of k lies between them.
